newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 17.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CROWN AGENTS GIVEN PRIVATE ROLE

The government is set to transfer the ownership of the Crown Agents, which buy goods and manage projects for foreign governments, to a new foundation whose members include British Telecom, Unilever, Barclays and several other major companies. The transfer will allow the Crown Agents to take on projects for the private sector, form joint ventures and return to investment.
-- ROVER PUTS FOOT DOWN TO STREAMLINE PRODUCTION

Rover is looking for major changes to its 'no compulsory redundancy' agreement with employees. It is also pressing suppliers to move faster to 'just in time' delivery practices. The drive by the BMW-owned car manufacturer is to raise productivity and cut costs and follows Rover's plans for a further run-down in the workforce at Longbridge and expansion at Land Rover.
-- GALLAHER PREPARES FOR 2 BILLION POUNDS DE-MERGER

Gallaher, the leading cigarette manufacturer in the UK, has finalised its board structure in the run-up to a 2 billion pounds stg de-merger from American Brands, the US parent. A Gallaher listing in London following the de-merger is expected in early summer. Shareholders in AMerican Brands, which is severing its links with tobacco and will be renamed Fortune Brands, will hold the shares initially, which will be quoted in London and New York.
THE TIMES
-- SFO TO MOVE OVER BANK'S BLACK HOLE

The Serious Fraud Office is to step up its monitoring of the 90 million pounds stg blackhole at NatWest Markets. The SFO have not yet been given enough evidence by NatWest that trades in the interest rate options market by Kyriacos Papouis, the former trader, involved criminal behaviour. There is no suggestion that Mr Papouis acted for personal gain and if this remains the position the SFO is expected to launch a formal inquiry only if it emerges that the data input into the investment banking group's computers or trading books amounted to making misleading statements or false accounting.
-- LITTLEWOODS STORES SALE TO SHAKE UP RETAILERS

A new report suggests that the sale of Littlewoods' stores could drastically alter the balance of power among Britain's clothing retailers. The survey from Verdict, the retail consultancy, says that if Asda bought the 135-strong chain it would increase competition at the lower end of the market, hitting both C&A and BhS. If Next buy the chain, the impact would be felt by Marks & Spencer. The report coincides with rumours that both Kingfisher and Tesco are thought to be considering bids for the stores.
-- BELEAGUERED SHELL TAKES STAND ON HUMAN RIGHTS

Shell is expected to announce today a drastic change to its business principles, and will incorporate a statement of support for fundamental human rights. The new version of the companies general business principles, is expected to state that the oil company has a duty to support human rights, has proper regard for the environment and a committment to sustainable development.
THE GUARDIAN
-- 'NAZI GOLD' BANK CHANGES NAME

Union Bank of Switzerland is to distance itself from the "Nazi gold" scandal by changing its name. The bank, one of the world's most powerful banks, plans to drop the word Switzerland and restyle itself simply as UBS. A team of executives have been working on the plan to rebrand the bank throughout the world.
-- FIRMS DENY THAT MINIMUM WAGE WOULD BE BAD FOR BUSINESS

A new survey reveals that nearly 80 per cent of firms believe they would be unaffected by a nimum wage of 3.25 pounds stg an hour. The study conducted by Reed Personnel Services is a boost for Labour's hopes of making the minimum wage a focal part of its general election strategy.
-- PEARSON TV PLAN IS BLOW FOR DYKE

Pearson's new chief executive, Marjorie Scardino, will today insist that the media and leisure group plan to keep its television operations. The decision will be a blow to Greg Dyke, head of Pearson's TV operations, who was believed to be considering heading a management buyout.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BUFFETT WARNS THAT WALL STREET MAY BE HEADING FOR A FALL

American investment guru, Warren Buffett has joined the increasing number of analysts warning that stock prices in the US are too high. In a letter to shareholders in his publicly quoted investment company, Berkshire Hathaway, he says that the risk of overpayment may now be quite high for purchasers of virtually all stocks.
-- WORLD-WIDE SURGE IN STATE SELL-OFFS TO BRING IN 100 BILLION
DOLLARS

Privatisation receipts world-wide could reach 100 billion dollars US this year according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. A global surge in selling off state assets is having a profound effect on capital markets, particularly equity markets, the report claims. Privatisation may also facilitate a switch from investment in bonds to investments in equities.
-- BBC TAKES PLUNGE INTO PAY-TV WITH FLEXTECH

The BBC is expected to announce today a joint venture with Flextech to provide five new pay-television channels. The statement is expected to confirm the BBC's first substantive step into the world of commercial television, with Flextech putting up 22 million pounds stg of equity and its parent company TCI guaranteeing loan facilities of up to 118 million pounds stg.
